from.place: Proof paragraph 2 of prop-coef-integral-exceptional-adjoint in main-20261015: the finite-level mapping-complex adjunction; supporting operadic algebra-category invariance in the inherited enrichment ancestry, realized by the categorical-fibration, slice and relative Kan-extension argument of Gepner–Haugseng A.6.5.

title: Algebra categories are invariant under color-equivalent weak approximation
statement:
Use the infinity-category and universe conventions of [def-coef-complete-algebroid] and the ordinary and generalized nonsymmetric infinity operads of [lem-coef-operadic-algebra-presentability]. Let $f:M\to O$ be an inert-preserving map from a small generalized nonsymmetric infinity operad to a small ordinary nonsymmetric infinity operad. Suppose $f$ is a weak approximation in the sense of [def-coef-operadic-weak-approximation] and $f_{[1]}:M_{[1]}\to O_{[1]}$ is an equivalence of infinity categories. Then for every ordinary nonsymmetric infinity operad $P$, restriction induces an equivalence of infinity categories
$$f^*:\operatorname{Alg}_O(P)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Alg}_M(P).$$
Here $\operatorname{Alg}_Q(P)$ is the full subcategory of the functor infinity category over $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ on inert-preserving functors $Q\to P$, with all coherent transformations. No space hypothesis on the color category of $O$ is required; the zero-fiber convention of the cited generalized-operad definition remains in force.

source.place: Theorem A.6.5 (equivalence of full algebra infinity categories, not only their cores) Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this infinity-operadic result.

proof.text: Factor $f$ as $M\xrightarrow{e}C\xrightarrow{g}O$ using [def-coef-operadic-weak-approximation], with $e$ an equivalence of generalized operads and $g$ a categorical-fibration weak approximation. The unary-fiber restriction of $e$ is an equivalence, so $g_{[1]}$ is an equivalence by composing quasi-inverses. A quasi-inverse to $e$ over $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, and its coherent inverse transformations, give inverse precomposition functors on the full functor categories over the base. They restrict to inert-preserving objects because both directions of an operadic equivalence preserve inert edges. Thus it suffices to prove the assertion for $g:C\to O$. Write $B=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, $p:O\to B$ and $q:P\to B$. Both inner fibrations $p$ and $q$ are isofibrations: every equivalence of $B$ is an identity and has an identity lift.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23(1), reduction to a categorical fibration; nonsymmetric version is Gepner–Haugseng A.6.5.

proof.text: Apply the opposite of [lem-coef-cocartesian-straightening] to the diagram $C\xrightarrow{g}O$ indexed by $(\Delta^1)^{\mathrm{op}}$. Obtain a Cartesian fibration $u:E\to\Delta^1$ with $E_0=O$ and $E_1=C$. For $c\in C$, its Cartesian edge is $g(c)\to c$. The Cartesian mapping-square criterion identifies the space of cross-fiber edges $X\to c$ with $\operatorname{Map}_O(X,g(c))$, compatibly with compositions: restrict that square to the base edge $0\to1$, whose mapping space is a point. Thus $C\times_E E_{X/}$ identifies with $O_{X/}\times_O^h C$, including coherent triangles. The colimit of the arrow $C\to O$ is $O$: a cocone to $T$ is a functor $O\to T$ together with its already specified composite from $C$, so its universal comparison is an equivalence. Hence [lem-coef-cartesian-colimit-localization] supplies $r:E\to O$, with $r|_O=1$, $r|_C=g$, and an equivalence $\operatorname{Fun}(O,T)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathrm{Cart}(u)}(E,T)$ for every target $T$. Put $s=pr:E\to B$. These are coherent constructions over $B$; they may be represented with the prescribed endpoint restrictions strictly, using the exponential isofibration of [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation].

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.266: Cartesian cylinder and retraction; generic construction via Cartesian straightening.

proof.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}_s(E,P)$ on functors $F$ such that $F|_O$ is an $O$-algebra and $F$ sends every $u$-Cartesian edge to an equivalence. Apply the preceding localization equivalence both to $T=P$ and to $T=B$, and take its fiber at $p:O\to B$, corresponding to $s:E\to B$. This gives an equivalence of the functor categories over these base maps. To justify using degreewise fibers, postcomposition by the isofibration $q$ is an isofibration by [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation], and [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-pullback-limit] identifies its degreewise fibers with the infinity-categorical fibers. Restricting to the stated full subcategories gives $r^*:\operatorname{Alg}_O(P)\simeq\mathcal X$, with inverse restriction to $O$. In particular this equivalence retains noninvertible transformations; no inference from contractible object fibers is being made.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.266: the category X and its restriction to O.

proof.text: Fix an algebra $A:C\to P$ and $X\in O_{[n]}$. Set $K_X=C\times_E E_{X/}\simeq O_{X/}\times_O^h C$. Its objects are edges $a:X\to g(c)$, and its arrows are coherent triangles induced by arrows of $C$. Let $I_X\subseteq K_X$ be the full subcategory where $a$ is an inert edge in $O$. For an object $a:X\to g(c)$ of $K_X$, the comma category $(I_X)_{/a}$ is exactly $\mathcal F_g(c,a)$: its objects are $b:d\to c$ and inert $h:X\to g(d)$ with $g(b)h\simeq a$, and its higher simplices are the compatible triangles in the definition. It is weakly contractible by [def-coef-operadic-weak-approximation]. The opposite form of [lem-coef-infinity-cofinal-comma-criterion], using the opposite conventions of [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-equivalence], therefore says that restriction from $K_X$ to $I_X$ induces equivalences of cone categories and of constant-source mapping spaces, both in $P$ and in $B$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.267: weak approximation gives the coinitial inert subcategory.

proof.text: Introduce a distinct full subcategory $H_X\subseteq K_X$: its objects are all $a:X\to g(c)$ whose BASE map is inert, without requiring $a$ to be cocartesian in $O$. Then $I_X\subseteq H_X\subseteq K_X$. For every object $a$ of $H_X$, its comma category under $I_X$ is the same $\mathcal F_g(c,a)$ as above, since $H_X$ is full. The same opposite comma criterion gives equivalences on cone categories and constant-source mapping spaces from $H_X$ to $I_X$. The restriction from $K_X$ to $I_X$ factors through $H_X$, so two-out-of-three gives these equivalences from $K_X$ to $H_X$ as well. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-constant-test] to the constant-source mapping-space squares in $P$ and $B$: a cone on $A|_{K_X}$ is a $q$-limit iff its restriction to $H_X$ is. A prescribed relative limit cone on $H_X$ extends to one on $K_X$: the equivalence of cone categories provides the extension up to equivalence, and the exponential corner isofibration rectifies its boundary and base cone to the prescribed ones. Here [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-pullback-limit] identifies the fixed-base cone category with that homotopy fiber. This also applies when the boundary category is empty.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.267: coinitiality, with distinct actual-inert and base-inert subcategories to correct the literal slice comparison.

proof.text: Let $J_X\subseteq H_X$ be the full subcategory with $c\in C_{[1]}$. For $a:X\to g(c)$ in $H_X$, with $c\in C_{[m]}$, the category $J_X\times_{H_X}(H_X)_{a/}$ is the disjoint union of the lift categories $L(c,\rho_j)$, $1\le j\le m$. Indeed a triangle is determined by its arrow $c\to d$; the opposite of the base of $a$ is $t\mapsto b+t$, so its composite with $\beta^{\mathrm{op}}:[1]\to[m]$ is a length-one interval inclusion exactly when $\beta^{\mathrm{op}}(1)-\beta^{\mathrm{op}}(0)=1$. Thus $\beta=\rho_j$. Every higher simplex has this same base arrow, giving the claimed decomposition on all simplices. By [lem-coef-operadic-algebra-presentability] choose an inert projection $c\to c_j$ in each component. It is initial there by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality]. Since $A$ is an algebra, the arrows $A(c)\to A(c_j)$ are inert. The ordinary target's product mapping-space axiom makes their discrete cone a $q$-limit: the dual constant-source test in [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-constant-test] has fibers over each base arrow precisely that product equivalence. Apply [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] to pass from this discrete cone to the whole comma diagram. Therefore $A|_{H_X}$ is the pointwise $q$-right Kan extension of $A|_{J_X}$ in [lem-coef-relative-right-kan-universal-restriction]. For $m=0$ the comma category is empty and the target's empty-product axiom gives the relative limit over $[0]$. No terminality of $C_{[0]}$ is used.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.267: right Kan extension from unary projections; replace the printed final-object wording by the cocartesian initial-object criterion.

proof.text: Decompose $J_X=\coprod_{i=1}^n J_{X,i}$ by the base projection $\rho_i:[n]\to[1]$. Put $O(X,i)=(O_{X/})\times_{B_{[n]/}}\{\rho_i\}$, with target functor to $O_{[1]}$. The cross-edge description of step 2 identifies $J_{X,i}$ with $O(X,i)\times^h_{O_{[1]}}C_{[1]}$. Pulling back a quasi-inverse and its coherent inverse transformations for $g_{[1]}$ shows that projection to $O(X,i)$ is an equivalence. Choose an inert projection $X\to X_i$ and $c_i\in C_{[1]}$ with $X_i\simeq g(c_i)$. The resulting inert edge $a_i:X\to g(c_i)$ is initial in $O(X,i)$ by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality], applied to $p:O\to B$. It therefore defines an initial object of $J_{X,i}$: the displayed equivalence identifies all mapping spaces, by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. This also treats empty color categories: an $X$ with $n>0$ supplies the required colors through its projections; if no colors exist there are no such $X$. For $n=0$, $J_X$ is empty.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed pp.267–268: case (1), unary slices, product existence and criterion (b prime).

proof.text: Choose $Y\in P_{[n]}$ with inert projections to the objects $A(c_i)$, using the Segal equivalence $P_{[n]}\simeq P_{[1]}^n$ of [lem-coef-operadic-algebra-presentability]. For $n=0$ this is the unique empty tuple. These projections give a $q$-limit over the restriction of the prescribed base cone to the discrete set of $a_i$: the ordinary-operad mapping-space product axiom, tested over every base arrow, is exactly the homotopy-pullback square in the dual of [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-constant-test]. Apply [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] to the initial objects of step 7 to obtain a $q$-limit cone with the specified boundary on all of $J_X$. Step 6 and the cone-comparison clause of [lem-coef-relative-right-kan-universal-restriction] extend it to a $q$-limit on $H_X$, retaining its apex and its legs on $J_X$. Step 5 then extends it to $K_X$. All indexing categories are small. This proves existence of the relative limits required for the extension construction.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed pp.267–268: case (1), unary slices, product existence and criterion (b prime).

proof.text: A specified cone on $K_X$ over the prescribed base is limiting if and only if its legs to the selected $A(c_i)$ are inert. Indeed, step 5 reduces its universal property to its restriction to $H_X$; step 6 and the cone-comparison clause of [lem-coef-relative-right-kan-universal-restriction] reduce that to its restriction to $J_X$; and [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] reduces this to the discrete cone. Inert legs give a $q$-limit by the ordinary-operad product mapping-space axiom of [lem-coef-operadic-algebra-presentability] and the dual constant-source test of [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-constant-test]. Conversely compare a limiting discrete cone to the tuple cone of step 8. Testing the two universal properties at their apices gives inverse comparison maps over $1_{[n]}$, with the prescribed legs; their composites are homotopic to identities by the same mapping-space equivalences. Thus its legs are the tuple projections composed with an equivalence, and are inert by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion]. This test is independent of choices. Every inert unary edge $a:X\to g(c)$ over $\rho_i$ is initial in $O(X,i)$ by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality], hence in $J_{X,i}$ by step 7. The comparison with $a_i$ is an equivalence retaining its triangle. Its image under $A$ is an equivalence, so the corresponding cone legs differ by postcomposition with an equivalence. The mapping criterion preserves and reflects inertness under this operation. Thus the criterion holds for every inert unary cross-edge, and testing one for each $i$ suffices; for $n=0$ the test is empty.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed pp.267–268: case (1), unary slices, product existence and criterion (b prime).

proof.text: Let $\mathcal R\subseteq\operatorname{Fun}_s(E,P)$ be the full subcategory on pointwise $q$-right Kan extensions whose restriction to $C$ is an algebra. The inclusion $C\subseteq E$ is full. For a vertex of the $O$-fiber, steps 7–9 supply the required relative limit on $K_X=C\times_E E_{X/}$. For a vertex $c$ of the $C$-fiber, this comma category is $C_{c/}$ with initial object $1_c$, and the canonical cone with apex $A(c)$ is the required relative limit: evaluation at $1_c$ identifies constant-source cone mapping spaces with maps to $A(c)$, and identifies the relative-limit test square with the identity square over the prescribed base cone. The target $q$ is an isofibration by step 1; all shapes are small. Thus [lem-coef-relative-right-kan-universal-restriction] applies and gives an equivalence $\mathcal R\to\operatorname{Alg}_C(P)$, in fact the stated trivial Kan fibration, on all transformations and higher simplices. The extension criterion from step 9 says that $F\in\mathcal R$ iff $F|_C$ is an algebra and, for every $X\in O_{[n]}$, the maps $F(X)\to F(c)$ along every inert unary cross-edge $X\to c$ are inert; by step 9 it suffices to test one such edge over each $\rho_i$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed pp.266–268: assertions (a) and (b prime), applied via HTT 4.3.2.15.

proof.text: If $F\in\mathcal X$, its images of the Cartesian edges $g(c)\to c$ give a coherent equivalence $(F|_O)g\simeq F|_C$. The factor $g$ is a map of generalized nonsymmetric operads in the factorization of [def-coef-operadic-weak-approximation], so it preserves inert edges; $F|_O$ preserves them, and composing with the componentwise equivalence $(F|_O)g\simeq F|_C$ preserves the cocartesian mapping-square criterion. Hence $F|_C$ is an algebra. For any chosen inert cross-edge $X\to c_i$, its factorization in $E$ is the inert edge $X\to g(c_i)$ followed by the Cartesian edge $g(c_i)\to c_i$. The image of the former is inert since $F|_O$ is an algebra, and the latter is an equivalence. The composite is inert: postcomposition by an equivalence preserves the cocartesian mapping-square criterion. Consequently step 10 gives $F\in\mathcal R$. These statements include all arities; at arity zero the product criterion is the empty one.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.268: forward direction of (b).

proof.text: Conversely let $F\in\mathcal R$. For $c\in C_{[m]}$ choose inert projections $c\to c_j$; $F(c)\to F(c_j)$ are inert because $F|_C$ is an algebra. For $X=g(c)$ the extension criterion of step 10 makes all the composite maps $F(g(c))\to F(c)\to F(c_j)$ inert. These are two $q$-product cones over the same unary objects and the same base cone, so the comparison $F(g(c))\to F(c)$ is an equivalence. Explicitly, the product mapping-space axiom identifies the comparison on each mapping-space fiber with the identity of the product of the unary mapping spaces; the inverse comparisons supplied by the two universal properties have identity composites by uniqueness. For $m=0$ both objects are the relative terminal object over $[0]$, giving the same conclusion. Every Cartesian edge of $u$ factors as a Cartesian lift $g(c)\to c$ and an equivalence in a fiber, or is already an equivalence in a fiber; its image is therefore an equivalence. This proves condition (ii) for $\mathcal X$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.268: reverse direction of (b), inversion of Cartesian edges.

proof.text: For an inert edge $a:X\to Y$ of $O$, over $\alpha:[n]\to[k]$, choose inert unary projections $Y\to Y_j$ and identifications $Y_j\simeq g(c_j)$ supplied by $g_{[1]}$. The cross-edges $Y\to c_j$ and $X\to Y\to c_j$ correspond to inert edges of $O$, since the composite of their cocartesian mapping squares is a homotopy-pullback square and their base maps are consecutive interval projections. Thus step 10 makes $\beta_j:F(Y)\to F(c_j)$ and $\beta_jF(a):F(X)\to F(c_j)$ inert. Choose a cocartesian inert lift $u:F(X)\to Z$ of $\alpha$ and factor $F(a)=vu$ with $v:Z\to F(Y)$ over $1_{[k]}$, by the cocartesian mapping-square criterion. Choose inert projections $z_j:Z\to Z_j$. Both $z_ju$ and $\beta_jvu$ are cocartesian over $\rho_j\alpha$. Comparing their universal mapping squares gives an equivalence $t_j:Z_j\to F(c_j)$ over $1_{[1]}$ with $t_jz_ju\simeq\beta_jvu$. Precomposition with $u$ is an equivalence on the relevant mapping-space fibers, so $t_jz_j\simeq\beta_jv$. Under the Segal equivalence $P_{[k]}\simeq P_{[1]}^k$, with the unary components of $F(Y)$ identified with $F(c_j)$ by $\beta_j$, these $t_j$ are precisely the components of $v$. They are equivalences, so $v$ is an equivalence. For $k=0$, the fiber $P_{[0]}$ is contractible and $v$ is an equivalence without unary tests. Composing $u$ with $v$ preserves its cocartesian mapping square, so $F(a)$ is inert. Hence $F|_O$ is an algebra and $F\in\mathcal X$. Together with step 12 this proves $\mathcal R=\mathcal X$ as full subcategories.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, printed p.268: reverse direction of (b), preservation of all inert arrows.

proof.text: Compose $\operatorname{Alg}_O(P)\xrightarrow{r^*}\mathcal X=\mathcal R\xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}_C}\operatorname{Alg}_C(P)$. Steps 3 and 10 show both functors are equivalences of the full infinity categories. Since $r|_C=g$, the composite is exactly $g^*$. Finally $f^*=e^*g^*$, and the inverse precomposition equivalence from step 1 proves the required equivalence for $f$. Composition of coherent functors makes this identification on every simplex, so no noninvertible transformation has been discarded. Restriction commutes with postcomposition into every ordinary target operad by associativity of composition, also on transformations and their higher simplices.

proof_origin.place: Agent-written nonsymmetric adaptation of Higher Algebra (2017), Theorem 2.3.3.23(1), printed pp.266–268, as referred to by Gepner–Haugseng Theorem A.6.5 (read online). The detailed HA proof is not archived locally and subsequent online proof-page reads timed out. Q123 retains the reviewed Cartesian-cylinder/right-Kan argument and replaces the long unary-slice calculation by existing initial-components and cocartesian-lift nodes; see report.
